Introduction Dengue, a mosquito-borne viral disease, has been a significant public health burden in the tropical and subtropical areas since the early 20th century [15]. The causative agent for this disease is dengue virus, a single positive-stranded RNA virus of the family Flaviviridae, with strains characterized by five serotypes [36]. Dengue virus is primarily transmitted by female mosquitoes of the Aedes genus that includes species such as Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus [31]. At present, it is estimated that around 400 million people are infected with dengue annually, and about half a million require hospital care [3,22,36]. Common symptoms of dengue include sudden-onset fever, headache, vomiting, and a characteristic skin rash. Severe cases of dengue infection can cause health complications such as dengue haemorrhagic fever and dengue shock syndrome, which may lead to death if not treated in a timely manner [12]. Individuals infected with dengue virus will go through an exposed (or, latent) period of 3–8 days without exhibiting any symptoms [16]. These asymptomatic individuals can infect local mosquitoes which go on to bite other people and spread the infection to larger human populations. They also pose a threat to transfusion recipients through infected blood products [18]. Furthermore, asymptomatic individuals can be re-infected, referred to as a secondary infection, through mosquitoes carrying a different strain of dengue virus and become symptomatic with more severe health conditions [24]. The mechanism for the different viral serotypes to cause severe dengue disease is not entirely clear at present, but it is mostly linked to the Antibody-Dependent Enhancement (ADE), a phenomenon where pre-existing antibodies do not neutralize but rather enhance the new infection [2]. Hence, asymptomatic infectious individuals play a significant role in shaping the overall pattern of dengue transmission and spread. Quantifying such a role is essential in understanding the transmission dynamics of dengue and in designing effective prevention and intervention strategies. Like many other infectious disease, the transmission of dengue exhibits strong heterogeneity among different human hosts. One of the most important factors to reflect such heterogeneity is the chronological age. Individuals of different ages may have different social behaviors, mobility levels, and contact dynamics, which subsequently lead to different infection risk, disease severity, survival capacity, and recovery ability. In particular, children are more vulnerable than adults because of their immature immune systems, and they have higher risk of severe complications for dengue [28,33]. Identifying such transmission characteristics associated with different age groups and classifying such an age structure in a dengue model are critical toward a holistic understanding of dengue transmission dynamics. Numerous mathematical models have been published for the transmission dynamics of dengue [1,11– 13,16,18–20,22,24,26,29,31]. For example, Esteva and Vargas studied the coexistence of different serotypes of dengue virus [11].
